evidence: CDIAL 4008 gata explicitly supplies the go-preterite: Prakrit gaya/gaa, Hindi gayā and Old Marwari gayaü, with contracted Old Gujarati gyau. These simple past forms belong to the suppletive gata family rather than the jā- present stem.
CDIAL 1045 āgata gives Prakrit āya, Hindi āyā and Old Marwari āīyo. These simple arrived/came forms select the inherited preterite rather than the āv- present or the two-part ā-gayā construction.
CDIAL 6140.3 *dita specifically gives Hindi diyā and Nepali diyo ‘given’. This identifies the past participial branch, distinct from the present de- family.

Pali mattha/matthaka and Prakrit mattha lead to Hindi māthā and explicitly Marwari mātho ‘head, forehead’. The dental aspirate and vowel length fit the first branch of masta/mastaka; no brain-related subsection is intended.
CDIAL gives Hindi bāl, Gujarati vāḷ and Bhojpuri bār ‘hair’ beneath vāla. Initial v > b and the regional lateral variants have explicit comparanda.
CDIAL gives Hindi bāl, Gujarati vāḷ and Bhojpuri bār ‘hair’ beneath vāla. Initial v > b and, in Bagheli bar, the regional l/r correspondence have explicit comparanda.
Prakrit kaṇṇa corresponds to Hindi, Old Marwari, Gujarati and Marathi kān ‘ear’ in CDIAL. The local dental/retroflex nasal and variable written vowel length fit this inherited family.

CDIAL explicitly gives Hindi, Marwari, Gujarati and Marathi dā̃t from danta. Reduction of nt with vowel lengthening/nasalisation accounts for these forms; survey notation varies in whether nasalisation is written.
Prakrit jibbhā and Hindi jīb(h), Gujarati jībh and Marathi jībh are cited under jihvā. The reduced labial cluster fits the selected jib response.
Prakrit jibbhā and Hindi jīb(h), Gujarati jībh and Marathi jībh are cited under jihvā. The reduced labial cluster fits jib; Nimadi jip additionally shows final devoicing.
CDIAL’s first branch has Prakrit peṭṭa/piṭṭa and Hindi peṭ, Old Marwari peṭa, Gujarati peṭ; Maithili peṭ(h) also supplies an aspirated comparator. This is the e/i-vowel branch, separate from pōṭṭa.
CDIAL’s third branch explicitly gives Prakrit poṭṭa/puṭṭa and Marathi poṭ ‘belly’. The o vowel motivates this specific subsection rather than the peṭṭa head.
Prakrit haḍḍa, Hindi haḍḍā/haḍḍī and hāṛ, and Gujarati/Marathi hāḍ give direct comparanda. Turner explicitly calls a connection to asthi very doubtful; the proposal stops at haḍḍa.
CDIAL lists Prakrit gāma, Gujarati gām, Marwari gā̃v and Hindi gā̃u beneath grāma. The nasal and v/u outcomes are directly represented, without assigning the separate dehāt or khelo responses.
CDIAL gives Prakrit kuhaṇī, Hindi kohnī/kuhnī/kehunī, Gujarati kɔṇī and Nepali kuinu. These supply both the medial-h and contracted/metathesised comparanda for the local forms.
Prakrit akkhi/acchi corresponds to Hindi ā̃kh, Bhojpuri ākhⁱ and Old Marwari ākhi in CDIAL. Cluster reduction, vowel length and optional nasalisation fit the selected forms.

Prakrit ṇakka, Hindi/Gujarati/Marathi nāk and Kumaoni nākh are explicit comparanda under *nakka. Turner’s proposed deeper *nas-ka/*nast-ka origin is uncertain; the assignment stays at the attested comparative *nakka family.
Prakrit muha and Hindi muh/mũh, Bhojpuri mũh and Gujarati mõh appear under mukha ‘mouth, face’. The weakened kh and loss or retention of final h fit these selected mouth responses.
CDIAL explicitly gives Hindi/Marwari hāth ‘hand, arm, cubit’ and Marathi hāt. The arm/hand semantic range is primary-source evidence, and inherited st > tth > th/t explains the stem.
CDIAL 6225 gives Prakrit dōra/dōrī/ḍōra and Hindi, Bihari, Gujarati and Marathi dorī/ḍorī ‘rope, string’. The dental/retroflex variation is already represented in the family.
CDIAL 10582 gives Prakrit lajju, Hindi lej/lejur ‘rope’ and Bhojpuri lajurī ‘well-rope’. The l-for-r family is directly attested; no hypothetical modern Sanskrit loan is needed.

CDIAL 2485 ekādaśa gives Prakrit egārasa, Hindi igārah, Old Gujarati igyāra, Gujarati agyār and the Kotgarhi addendum’s gyāra. Loss of the initial vowel and the -dasa→-rasa→-rah/-ra history are supported within the full numeral family; the source’s final-vowel variants are retained as numeral forms.

CDIAL 6658.1 dvādaśa gives Prakrit bārasa/bāraha, Awadhi/Hindi/Old Marwari bārā, Bhojpuri bārē and Gujarati bār. The initial b- selects the first branch, not duvādaśa (section 2); loss of medial s/h and the final-vowel variants are directly supported.
CDIAL 2575 kaḥ punar gives Apabhramsha kavaṇa, Old Marwari kõṇa/kuṇa, Gujarati kɔṇ, Maithili kon and Hindi kaun. The nasal-ending interrogatives have direct regional comparanda.
CDIAL 3167 compares Prakrit kittiya, Hindi kittā/kitā and the addenda’s ketti ‘how much, how many’. The geminate or simplified t forms fit the base *kiyatta family.

CDIAL 8330 compares Hindi pūrā, Old Marwari puraü, Gujarati pūrũ and Marathi purā ‘full, complete’; Shina pūrṷ also means ‘all’. The selected whole/all meanings and ordinary gender forms are compatible.
CDIAL 4424 compares Sindhi ghaṇo ‘much, many’, Old Gujarati ghaṇauṁ ‘much’, and Marwari ghaṇo ‘big’. The dense-to-abundant sense development is explicitly attested.
CDIAL 992 aham gives Apabhramsha haü̃, Old Marwari hũ/hu and Gujarati hũ. This directly supports the h-initial first-person nominative.
CDIAL 5889.1 gives Prakrit tuṁ and Hindi/Old Marwari tū. The bare informal singular tu fits this nominative branch.
CDIAL 9209.1 compares Prakrit bappa and Hindi, Gujarati and Marathi bāp ‘father’. This is the bāppa nursery-word family; the separate bābba branch is not required.
CDIAL 10016 gives Prakrit māyā/māi, Hindi mā/māī/maiyā, Old Marwari mā (oblique māya), and Gujarati mā/māi. These reduced and y-bearing forms support the mātṛ family directly.
CDIAL 9349 compares Prakrit bahiṇī, Hindi bahin/bahan, Gujarati bahen/ben and Old Marwari bahaṇa. The standalone forms fit this family; age-marked compounds are excluded.
CDIAL 9661 traces Hindi and Marwari bhāī and Gujarati bhāi through Prakrit bhāi/bhāia. The merged older/younger senses refer to the same unmodified kinship word.
Compare Hindi/Marwari bhāī and Prakrit bhāi in CDIAL 9661. Both source senses are compatible with the unmodified term ‘brother’.

CDIAL 5070.1 compares Prakrit chōyara, Nepali choro/chorī, Hindi chorā/chorī and Gujarati chorɔ/chorī. The lost intervocalic velar and masculine/feminine endings match; all grouped source meanings denote children.
CDIAL 9238.2 specifically gives *bēṭṭa, with Hindi beṭā/beṭī and Marwari beṭo/beṭī. This is the child branch, not the root entry *biḍḍa ‘defective’.
CDIAL 10702 gives Prakrit rattī/rāī, Hindi rāt/rātī, Old Marwari rāti and Gujarati/Marathi rāt. Loss of the cluster and final-vowel variation match these regional comparanda.
CDIAL 242 gives Prakrit ajja, Apabhramsha ajju, Hindi/Marwari āj and eastern āji alongside Nepali āju. These provide both the palatal outcome of dy and the attested final-vowel variants.

CDIAL 12452 explicitly gives Pali/Prakrit sira, Maithili and Awadhi sir, Hindi sir, Gujarati sir/sar and Marathi śir. This is the śiras family with final-s loss, not the separate śīrṣa head; the attested sir and meaning match directly.

CDIAL 4423 ghaná ‘club, hammer’ explicitly gives Prakrit ghaṇa ‘hammer’ and Punjabi, Gujarati and Marathi ghaṇ ‘sledgehammer’. The retained initial aspiration and retroflex nasal match these western comparanda; the survey’s broader hammer meaning is compatible.
CDIAL 5260 gives Prakrit juṇṇa, Old Awadhi jūna, Hindi jūnā and Gujarati jūnũ ‘old’. The assimilated rṇ cluster, with singleton/geminate and gender-ending variation, fits these forms.
CDIAL 8283 compares Prakrit purāṇa, Hindi purānā, Bhojpuri purān and Gujarati purāṇũ. These support the old adjective with regional final endings; the source’s r/ṛ and n/ṇ distinctions are retained.
CDIAL 6983 gives Prakrit ṇa(v)a, Old Awadhi nava, Marwari navo and Gujarati navũ. The retained v distinguishes these from the y-bearing naviya family.
CDIAL 7025.2 specifically gives naviya, Prakrit ṇavia, Hindi/Bihari nayā and Old Marwari nayaü. The y-bearing stem fits this subsection rather than the unsplit navya head.
CDIAL 12548 compares Prakrit sukkha/sukka, Hindi sūkhā/sūkā, Gujarati sūkũ and Marathi sukā. Assimilation of ṣk and the attested aspiration variation account for this dry-adjective group.

CDIAL 12548 compares Prakrit sukkha/sukka and western sūk- forms. The primary Malvi survey independently aligns h-initial ‘dry’, ‘seven’, ‘hundred’ and ‘hear’ at Jesingpura, Bhunyakhedi, Jamli and Chandukhedi against s-initial Harsodan/Jhadmu; see the [locality comparison](../central-surveys-20260911/MALVI-S-H.md). This supports local s/ś > h rather than a distant donor.
CDIAL 10951 gives Prakrit laṁba, Hindi lambā/lā̃b, Old Marwari lāṁbaü and Gujarati lā̃bũ ‘long’. The labial cluster and gender endings match directly.
CDIAL 5679 traces hot adjectives through Pali/Prakrit tatta, with Hindi tātā, Marwari tāto and Gujarati tātũ. The pt > tt > t development provides direct support.
CDIAL 6495 gives Prakrit dūra, Hindi/Bhojpuri dūr, Old Awadhi dūri and Old Marwari durī. Both bare and vowel-final distance adverbs have direct regional comparanda.
CDIAL 10187.11 *mōṭṭa specifically compares Old Marwari moṭaü ‘big, fat’, Gujarati moṭũ and Marathi moṭā. This selects the relevant eleventh branch rather than root *muṭṭa ‘defective’.
CDIAL 9465 bhārika ‘heavy’ gives Bihari bhāri and Awadhi/Hindi/Gujarati/Marathi bhārī. The adjective belongs to this specific formation rather than the bare noun bhāra ‘load’.

CDIAL 3083 compares Prakrit kāla, Marwari kāḷo, Gujarati kāḷũ, Hindi kālā and Bihari/Bhojpuri kariyā. The l/r forms are represented in the family; this proposal does not claim an Indo-European origin for kāla itself.
CDIAL 6767 compares Old Gujarati dhaülaü, Gujarati dhɔḷũ, Hindi dhaulā/dhorā and Marathi dhavaḷ. Both contracted and v-bearing forms fit the dhavala ‘white’ family.

CDIAL gives Hindi *gehũ/gahũ/gohũ*, Gujarati *gahũ/ghaũ*, Marathi *gahũ* and Konkani *gaṃv* under *godhūma*. The h-retaining and more contracted western forms thus have explicit comparanda; the unrelated village homonym is excluded.

CDIAL specifies Hindi *kā̃dā*, Gujarati *kā̃dɔ* and Marathi *kā̃dā* ‘onion’ under *kanda* ‘bulbous root’. The source meaning therefore supports this family directly; Nimadi kānta additionally needs confirmation of the devoiced stop.
Prakrit *tēla/tella/tilla*, Hindi *tel* and Gujarati/Marathi *tel* continue *taila* ‘oil’. Prakrit tilla also supplies a comparator for Malvi tīl without assigning the sesame-seed noun *tila*.

CDIAL lists Prakrit *loṇa/lūṇa*, Marwari *lūṇ*, Marathi *loṇ*, Maithili *non* and Bhojpuri *nūn*. Both the lateral and initial-n variants are explicitly represented; the distinct namak loan family is excluded.
Prakrit *maṃsa/māsa*, Hindi/Marathi *mās/mā̃s* and Maithili *māsu* are cited beneath *māṃsa*. The nasalised and unnasalised forms have direct comparanda; merged meat/month records are excluded.
CDIAL gives Hindi *aṇḍā*, Marathi *ā̃ḍẽ* and Gujarati *ĩḍũ* ‘egg’ under *āṇḍa*. The front-vowel western forms are explicitly supported alongside the a-vowel egg forms.

CDIAL’s *gāvī* branch gives Prakrit *gāī*, Hindi *gāī*, Gujarati *gā/gāy*, Marathi *gāī* and Old Marwari *gāi*. The y/i-bearing forms specifically fit that feminine branch, rather than the masculine ox head.

Prakrit *duddha*, Hindi/Marwari *dūdh* and Marathi *dūdh* support *dugdha*; CDIAL also cites deaspirated *dud* and final-devoiced *dut*. Bagheli’s retroflex d notation is preserved as a qualification.

Prakrit *siṃga*, Hindi *sī̃g*, Gujarati *sĩg* and Marathi *śī̃g* occur under *śṛṅga*. The simplified initial cluster and retained or lost final g match this family; local extended -ḍ- forms are left for a separate analysis.

Prakrit *sappa*, Hindi *sāp/sā̃p*, Bhojpuri *sā̃p* and Gujarati/Marathi *sāp* directly support *sarpa*. The Bagheli aspirated sāph is retained provisionally pending confirmation; euphemistic animal names are not included.
CDIAL 1268 gives Pali/Prakrit amba, Hindi ām/ā̃b, Old Awadhi āṁba and Gujarati ā̃b/ām. Retained mb and its simplification both belong to the mango family. Final vowels accord with the western forms.

CDIAL 3193 gives Prakrit kīḍa/kīḍī/kīḍiyā ‘worm, insect, ant’, Hindi kīṛī and Gujarati kīṛī ‘ant’. The feminine/extended forms fit directly; masculine kiḍa may represent a broader insect word used for the elicited ant.
CDIAL 1340.2 specifically gives *ālla < *ārdla, Pali/Prakrit alla, Hindi ālā and Old Marwari ālo ‘wet’. It supplies the relevant l/geminate-l branch rather than an unexplained direct link to ārdra.
CDIAL 10539 gives Pali/Prakrit ratta, Hindi rātā and Gujarati rātũ ‘red’. The kt > tt > t development and adjective endings support this colour family.
CDIAL 6648 compares Prakrit dō/duvē, Hindi and Marwari do, and Bihari/Awadhi dui. Both contracted do and dui-type forms belong to the same numeral family.
CDIAL 5994.3 trīṇi gives Prakrit tiṇṇi, Hindi/Marwari tīn and Awadhi tīnⁱ. This selects the neuter-form branch, not the masculine trayaḥ head.

CDIAL 4655.2 catvāri gives Apabhramsha cāri, Hindi/Gujarati cār, Old Marwari cyāri and Awadhi cāri. Turner explicitly notes unusual contraction or analogical influence in the numeral; branch 2 is the matching source form.
CDIAL 7655 compares Prakrit paṁca and Hindi/Marwari/Gujarati/Awadhi pā̃c. The family is supported by the labial onset and palatal stop with nasal-consonant/nasal-vowel variation.
CDIAL 13139 gives Pali/Prakrit satta and Hindi/Marwari/Gujarati/Awadhi sāt. Assimilation of pt and simplification of the resulting geminate support the numeral.

CDIAL 13139 gives Prakrit satta and regional sāt. The primary survey has hat alongside h-initial ‘dry’, ‘hundred’ and ‘hear’ in the same localities, opposed to consistent s- in Harsodan/Jhadmu; see the [source matrix](../central-surveys-20260911/MALVI-S-H.md). The local correspondence supports this inherited numeral.
CDIAL 941 gives Pali/Prakrit aṭṭha, Hindi/Marwari/Gujarati āṭh and Bengali āṭ. These establish the retroflex stop and the attested aspirated/unaspirated outcomes.

CDIAL 6984 nava ‘nine’ compares Hindi/Awadhi nau, Old Marwari nova and Gujarati/Marathi nav. This is the numeral entry, distinct from nava ‘new’. Contracted and v-bearing variants belong to the same family.
CDIAL 6227 compares Prakrit dasa/daha and Hindi/Marwari/Gujarati/Awadhi das, with ś retained in some other regions. The numeral is daśa, not the derived daśaka or unrelated daṁśa.
CDIAL 11616 gives Prakrit vīsaṁ/vīsā, Hindi/Bhojpuri/Awadhi bīs, Old Marwari bīsa and Gujarati/Marathi vīs. Both b- and v- initials are directly represented in the regional numeral.

CDIAL 12278 compares Old Marwari sau and Gujarati sɔ. Survey ho occurs in the same localities as h-initial ‘dry’, ‘seven’ and ‘hear’, contrasting with s- localities; the [four-family source comparison](../central-surveys-20260911/MALVI-S-H.md) supplies the needed local s/ś > h evidence.
CDIAL 12278 compares Prakrit saya/saa, Hindi/Old Marwari sau and Gujarati sɔ. Loss of intervocalic t with subsequent vowel contraction supports the hundred family.

CDIAL 3865.1 gives Prakrit khāaï/khāi, Hindi khānā, Marwari khābo and Gujarati khāvũ. These selected khā-/khā-o imperatives contain the eating stem and an ordinary imperative ending; compound completives are excluded.
The bare imperative khā matches the regional eating stem in CDIAL 3865.1 (Hindi khānā, Marwari khābo). Paired responses with auxiliaries are not included.
CDIAL 3865.2 khādita compares Prakrit khāyita and Hindi khāyā ‘ate’. This selected past form belongs with the participial branch; it is not grouped under the present khādati.

CDIAL 8209 compares Prakrit pi(v)aï, Hindi pīnā, Gujarati pīvũ and Marathi piṇẽ. These selected imperative/infinitive forms continue the drinking stem; pī-l- completives and ambiguous bare past forms are excluded.

CDIAL 13902 compares Prakrit sō(v)aï, Hindi sonā, Awadhi sōwab and Old Marwari soaï. The v/y forms continue this present-stem family with ordinary inflection; the inherited sūt-/hūt- participle is a different branch.

CDIAL 13902 explicitly gives Bengali soyā ‘sleep, lie down’ and Assamese xoiba ‘lie down’, alongside the central sō- family. The selected simple soya has the same compatible posture sense; auxiliary-bearing responses are excluded.

CDIAL 6141 derives regional de- from Middle Indo-Aryan dēti/dēi, remodeled with imperative dēhi and the ‘take’ paradigm. The bare imperative belongs here; diyā and doubled de-de are excluded from this proposal.

CDIAL 4721 *calyati gives Prakrit callaï, Marwari cālṇo and Gujarati cālvũ. The explicitly long ā favors this geminate-derived branch over short-vowel calati; the selected forms contain no auxiliary.
CDIAL 10452 gives Prakrit jāi, Hindi jānā, Old Marwari jāvaï (imperative jā) and Gujarati javũ. These selected simple imperative forms belong to yāti; suppletive gayo/gya past forms are excluded.

CDIAL 1200 specifically compares Prakrit āvaï ‘comes’, Hindi ānā with stem āw-, Old Marwari āvaï and Gujarati āvvũ under āpayati. The selected come-imperatives belong here, while āyo past forms and ā-ja compounds require separate analysis.

CDIAL 9321 gives Prakrit bollaï, Hindi bolnā, Old Marwari bolaï and Gujarati bolvũ. Only simple inflections of bol- are grouped (both members in selected Nimadi pairs); the remote origin of *bōll is debated in the article and is not asserted here.

CDIAL 12598 gives Pali suṇāti, Prakrit suṇaï, Hindi sunnā, Marwari suṇṇo and Awadhi sunab. Selected forms and pairs contain the same listening stem with ordinary inflections; sun-li- and auxiliary-bearing responses are excluded.

CDIAL 12598 compares Marwari suṇṇo and Prakrit suṇaï. The primary survey’s h-initial hear imperatives align geographically with h in ‘dry’, ‘seven’ and ‘hundred’, versus s- at Harsodan/Jhadmu; see the [source matrix](../central-surveys-20260911/MALVI-S-H.md). Simple huṇ- forms therefore have independent local correspondence evidence.
CDIAL 12732 connects Prakrit laṇha with Punjabi nannhā, Gujarati nānũ and Braj nānhau ‘small’. The short/small senses fit the tender/small family.

CDIAL’s first branch explicitly includes Hindi *māch/māchī*, Old Marwari *maṃchā/maṃchī* and Prakrit *maccha*. These central reflexes are distinct from the *matsiya* subsection whose primary comparanda are northwestern.

CDIAL gives Prakrit *kukkuḍa/kukkuḍī*, Hindi *kukaṛ/kukṛī* and Gujarati *kukṛɔ/kukṛī* for cock/hen. The male and female local forms continue this expressive family; the separate murg- loan responses are excluded.
CDIAL cites Hindi *bakrā/bakrī*, Gujarati/Marathi *bākrā/bākrī* and Bihari *bakkar*. The reduced medial cluster and female ending fit the selected bárkara-family goat forms.
CDIAL separately reconstructs *kuttira* for Gujarati *kutrɔ*, Marathi *kutrā* and Western Pahari *kutar*. The r-bearing survey forms fit that specific extension rather than the plain *kutta* head.

CDIAL gives Hindi *bā̃dar*, Marwari *bā̃dro*, Gujarati *vā̃dar/vā̃drɔ* and Bihari *bānar* from *vānara*. The b/v and presence/absence of intrusive d have explicit comparanda; Bagheli retroflexion and some contractions remain qualified.

CDIAL gives Gujarati *nām*, Old Marwari *nāva* and Marathi *nā̃v/nāv* beneath *nāman*. Both m and v outcomes are therefore supported; the emphatic particle *nāma* (7064) is a separate entry and is not the parent.

Pali/Prakrit *ghara* and Hindi, Marwari, Gujarati and Marathi *ghar* directly match the house stem. Turner calls the deeper derivation from *gṛha* phonetically difficult; the proposal therefore stops at *ghara*.

Compare Hindi *chappar/chaprā* ‘sloping thatch, hut’, Gujarati *chāprũ* ‘thatched roof’ and the article’s Punjabi *chappar*. The local vowels and optional written aspiration fit the same roof word under *chattvara*.
CDIAL lists Hindi *kiwāṛ/kewāṛ*, Old Marwari *kibāṛi*, Gujarati *kamāṛ* and Marathi *kavāḍ*. These supply both the v/w and m variants and the retroflex stop/flap outcomes of *kavāṭa*.

CDIAL’s fourth branch has Prakrit *ukkhala/okkhala*, Hindi *ūkhal/okhlī*, Gujarati/Marathi *ukhaḷ* and Bihari *okhar*. These match the contracted mortar forms, rather than the distinct uncontracted *ulūkhala* branches.

CDIAL’s s-branch gives Prakrit *musala*, Hindi *musal/mūslī*, Gujarati *musḷũ*, Marathi *musaḷ* and Bihari *mūsar*. The l/ḷ/r and contracted forms are directly comparable, with no inference to the separate retroflex-sibilant branch.

CDIAL’s *hastakūṭa* article gives Hindi *hathauṛā/-ṛī*, Gujarati *hathɔṛɔ/athɔṛɔ* and Marathi *hatoḍā/-ḍī*. These directly support both the au/o contraction and the h-less Malvi variant; the forms continue the lexicalised compound.

Prakrit *sūī*, Hindi/Bihari *sūī*, Gujarati *soy* and Marathi *sūī* are explicitly in CDIAL’s first branch. The c-loss and resulting vowel sequence support these forms, separately from *suji* or nasalised c-retaining *sūñcī*.

CDIAL’s moon sense gives Prakrit *caṃda*, Hindi/Gujarati *cā̃d*, Hindi *candā* and Bhojpuri *cān*. The reduced cluster and nasal/stop variants support the selected forms; longer *candrama* responses are not included.
CDIAL puts Hindi/Marathi *tārā* and Gujarati *tārɔ* specifically in its masculine *tāraka* branch, rather than feminine *tārā*. The selected western forms match that branch directly.
Prakrit *pāṇia* and Hindi *pānī*, Marwari/Gujarati/Marathi *pāṇī* directly support the stem. The inherited vowel contraction and nasal variants match the selected forms.

Prakrit *pāṇia* and Hindi *pānī*, Marwari/Gujarati/Marathi *pāṇī* directly support the stem. Bagheli fronted *peni* is retained as a local vocalic variant; records merging rain with water are considered separately.
CDIAL 114 gives Prakrit aṁga ‘limb, body’ and Hindi/Gujarati/Marathi ā̃g ‘body’. Both body and limb senses are already explicit in the primary entry.
CDIAL explicitly gives Prakrit *aggi*, Old Marwari/Gujarati *āgi*, Hindi *āg/āgī* and Bhojpuri *āgī*. Simplification of gn through gg, with lengthening or retained final i, supports this fire family.

CDIAL gives Hindi *dhūā̃/dhuwā̃*, Bhojpuri *dhuā̃* and Gujarati *dhūvɔ* from *dhūma*. The weakened m and vowel hiatus are supported; the Bagheli retroflex d variants and some deaspirated forms warrant local phonetic confirmation.
Prakrit *rakkhā*, Hindi *rākh/rākhī* and Gujarati/Marathi *rākh* are listed under the ashes homonym *rakṣā*. The meaning selects this entry, not the separate ‘protection’ homonym.

The article groups *dhūli* with *dhūḍi* and explicitly cites Hindi *dhūl/dhūr*, Gujarati *dhūḷ/dhūṛ* and Marathi *dhūḷ*. These substantiate the lateral/rhotic variants; the Bagheli retroflex and deaspirated ḍul remains qualified.

Prakrit *patta/pattiā* and Hindi *pattā/pattī* ‘leaf’ are explicit under *pattra*. These dental-stop forms match; Malvi pān and the nasalised or retroflex-looking Nimadi forms require separate analysis.
CDIAL lists Prakrit *phulla* ‘flower’, Hindi *phūl*, Old Marwari *phūla* and Gujarati/Marathi *phūl*. The survey’s ph/ɸ variants fit this family, distinct from the fruit word *phala*.

CDIAL gives Hindi *phal*, Gujarati/Marathi *phaḷ*, and eastern *phar*. The ph/ɸ and l/ḷ variants are direct comparanda; Bagheli’s retained l and -ua extension leave Hindi contact or local derivation open.

The first branch of *kadala/kadalī* has Prakrit *kēla*, Hindi *kelā*, Bhojpuri *kerā* and Gujarati/Marathi *keḷ-* forms. Contraction and lateral/rhotic variation support this branch; the unrelated retroflex-d form *kaḍalī* is not selected.

CDIAL’s *kaṇṭaka* subsection gives Hindi/Marathi *kā̃ṭā*, Marathi *kāṭā*, Gujarati *kā̃ṭɔ* and Sindhi *kaṇḍo*. These substantiate the full-vowel thorn nouns, rather than automatically using the shorter *kaṇṭa* branch; merged ‘bite’ records are excluded.

CDIAL has Prakrit *vaddala* ‘cloud’, Hindi *bādal/bādar*, Bihari *bādar* and Gujarati/Marathi *vādaḷ*. Initial v/b and lateral/rhotic variants are directly supported; Bagheli’s retroflex d notation remains a phonetic qualification.
CDIAL 3196 explicitly replaces kīdṛk by *kādṛk, comparing Old Gujarati kaya ‘what?’ and Marathi kāy. This fits the y/diphthong forms; the separate kīdṛśa ‘what kind?’ formation is not used.

CDIAL 8330 compares Hindi pūrā, Old Marwari puraü, Gujarati pūrũ and Marathi purā ‘full, complete’; Shina pūrṷ also means ‘all’. The selected whole/all meanings and ordinary gender forms are compatible.
CDIAL 992 gives Apabhramsha haü̃, Braj haũ and Old Marwari hũ; the retained diphthong and nasalization support the aham nominative family.
CDIAL 5889.1 compares Prakrit tuṁ, Hindi tū and Marathi tũ. Both source politeness labels attach to the same form; politeness variation does not change the historical singular stem.
CDIAL 986 explicitly gives Hindi/Awadhi/Bhojpuri ham under asmad and Middle Indo-Aryan amhē. The same form serves both elicited clusivity categories in this survey.
CDIAL 9349 compares Prakrit bahiṇī, Hindi bahin/bahan, Gujarati bahen/ben and Old Marwari bahaṇa. The standalone forms fit this family; age-marked compounds are excluded.
CDIAL 9238.2 specifically gives *bēṭṭa, with Hindi beṭā/beṭī and Marwari beṭo/beṭī. This is the child branch, not the root entry *biḍḍa ‘defective’.

CDIAL 7540 includes nīcā ‘below’ and explicitly explains the widespread -cc- forms by influence of opposite ucca; it gives Old Marwari nīcaï ‘below’, Oriya nice and Gujarati nīcε adverbs. The survey adverb matches this low/below family; vowel length and final vowel variation are retained.

CDIAL’s first branch gives Prakrit *haliddā/haraddā*, Hindi *haldī/harad*, Gujarati/Marathi *haḷad* and eastern *hardī*. The local lateral/rhotic variants support *haridrā*, with the h-less Malvi form and Bagheli retroflex notation retained as qualifications.
CDIAL 14152 gives Prakrit hiaa, Old Marwari hiyaü and Marwari hīyo ‘heart’. Loss of medial d/y and contraction have direct western Indo-Aryan comparanda.
CDIAL 12732 compares Gujarati nānũ and Braj nānhau ‘small’, through Prakrit laṇha and n-initial remodeling. The dental/retroflex nasal distinction remains as transcribed.

CDIAL lists Hindi *bhaĩs/bhaĩsī*, Gujarati *bhẽś* and Old Marwari *bhaïṃsa/bhaïṃsi* under *mahiṣa*. These substantiate the characteristic mh > bh and contracted vowel outcomes; Malvi bhe/bes/bhems require additional local confirmation.

Prakrit *kutta*, Hindi *kuttā*, Marwari *kuto* and Gujarati *kuttɔ* are explicit comparanda. Turner calls the family expressive; Malvi katta and Bagheli’s retroflex notation retain local phonetic qualifications.
CDIAL 404 *anyākāra gives Hindi nyārā and Gujarati nyārũ ‘different, separate’. Final -e is compatible with ordinary inflection; the reconstructed compound is explicitly Turner’s hypothesis.
CDIAL 13119 gives Prakrit sarikkha and Hindi sarikā/sarīkhā, Old Marwari sārikho and Gujarati sarkhũ ‘like’. The elicited same meaning is compatible with the likeness adjective.
CDIAL 9634 gives Hindi, Maithili, Bengali and Gujarati bhor ‘dawn’. It offers *bhōrā alongside *bhōlā, and the r form selects the former without settling the family’s deeper origin.

The initial-l branch has Prakrit *lasuṇa/lasaṇa/lhasuṇa*, Hindi *lasun/lahsun/lassan*, Gujarati *lasaṇ* and Marathi *lasūṇ*. These explicitly support the contracted and h-bearing forms; learned ś-retention or contact is possible in the Malvi/Nimadi ś variants.

CDIAL 11165 gives Prakrit lohia, Hindi lohū/lahū and Gujarati lohī ‘blood’; contracted loi is attested in Kumauni/Garhwali and lui in other Indo-Aryan languages. The two vowel patterns have direct eastern/Hindi comparanda.

CDIAL gives Prakrit *camma* and Hindi/Marathi *cām* ‘hide, skin’ from *carman*. This unextended form belongs to the base entry; the survey’s cemeḍ-/cemṛ- forms are separately assigned to the existing *carmaḍa-* extension node.
CDIAL’s first branch gives Prakrit *kukkura*, Hindi *kukur/kūkar*, Bhojpuri *kukur* and Marwari *kukro*. These k-r forms belong to kurkura/kukkura, distinct from the kutt-/kutr- families.

CDIAL’s spider homonym *markaṭa* has Prakrit *makkaḍa*, Hindi *makṛī*, Bhojpuri *makarī* and Bengali *mākaṛ*. These support the medial simplification and retroflex stop/flap variants; kh-bearing forms retain an aspiration qualification.

CDIAL 2462.2 specifically assigns Hindi/Gujarati/Marathi ek and related forms to *ēkka. Turner leaves emphatic doubling versus an early Middle Indo-Aryan Sanskrit loan unresolved; the immediate *ēkka link preserves that uncertainty.

CDIAL 12803.3 specifically groups Pali/Prakrit cha, Punjabi che, Maithili chao and Marwari cha under *kṣaṭ or *kṣvaṭ. Preserve both reconstructions: the c/ch forms belong to this third branch, not root ṣaṣ or the *ṣuvaṭ branch.

CDIAL lists Hindi uṅglī, Gujarati ā̃gḷī, Marathi ãgḷī and Old Hindi ā̃gurī under aṅguli/aṅguri. Syncope and l/ḷ/r variation support this branch; survey-specific extended endings are retained in the proposal.

CDIAL gives Hindi camṛā, Gujarati cāmḍũ/cāmḍī and Marathi cāmḍẽ/cāmḍī as the historical -ḍ- extension of carman via camma. These survey forms fit that inherited extended family; the historical extension is supported, although local suffix productivity has not been established. Jambu has a dedicated historical extension node *carmaḍa- (4701-2), which is the selected parent.

CDIAL gives Hindi *pū̃ch/pūchī*, Gujarati *pũch* and Prakrit *puccha/puṃcha*. Its addenda distinguish a nasalised *puñcha* variant, but Jambu currently groups it here; the proposed link retains that family-level qualification.

CDIAL gives Hindi *macchar/māchar* and Gujarati *machrũ* under the mosquito homonym *matsara*. The family match is good, but the source explicitly questions the deeper relation to *makṣā*; local r/ḍ/ḷ and extended forms require phonetic/morphological qualification.

CDIAL 10816 retra gives Hindi ret/retī, Old Marwari reta and Gujarati retī ‘sand’. The addenda emphasize limited evidence for reconstructed tr; vowel/final extensions and Bagheli retroflex ṭ remain qualified.

CDIAL 11580 vālukā gives Prakrit vāluā, Hindi bālū/bārū and Gujarati vāḷu. Both l/r outcomes are represented; the noun branch is selected rather than 11579 vāluka ‘sandy’. Bagheli extended baluri and ṛ remain for local review.

CDIAL 3120 gives Hindi kāṭhī and Kachchi kāṭhī ‘wood’, with the wider kāṣṭha > kaṭṭha > kāṭh family. The survey’s dental t is preserved as a qualification; the meaning is wood used as fuel, not the unrelated kāṣṭhin ‘wooden’ adjective.

CDIAL 2333 reconstructs *uppari with emphatic consonant lengthening of upari, and explicitly gives Punjabi uppar, Hindi ūpar, Old Marwari upari/ūpara and Gujarati upar. The adverbial meaning selects 2333 rather than *uppara ‘upper’; local short vowels and final -o/-ā/-e are qualified regional/adverbial variants.

CDIAL 5071 gives Hindi choṭā, Awadhi choṭ and Gujarati choṭũ ‘small’. The addenda distinguish related *chōṭa/*cōṭa forms, so the deaspirated variants are grouped as a qualified small-word family rather than a proven unique reconstruction.

CDIAL 3104.2 kalya gives Prakrit kallaṃ/kalhiṃ and Hindi kal for yesterday/tomorrow, with long-vowel forms in Awadhi, Bengali, Gujarati and Marathi. The two temporal senses are explicitly compatible; source records retain their distinct elicited meanings. The specific short-vowel Sanskrit branch is selected, while local vowel length and final-e need review.
